title: How to Disagree Without Becoming a Detractor
author: Karol Wójciszko
summary: Engineering manager Karol Wójciszko argues that most reasons people give for quitting, such as a clueless manager, a senseless strategy or shifting priorities, exist in every company and so follow people to the next job. He observes that middle managers, the C-level and engineers each see incompetence in the layer above or below, which he treats as a feature of how organisations compress information and context rather than a flaw in one company. His own practice is to disagree clearly and out loud to the decision makers, once or maybe twice, and then to follow the chosen strategy as if it were his own, a habit he links to Amazon's disagree and commit. He warns that people who keep lobbying one by one become detractors, which damages their reputation and splits execution across competing strategies. A well-executed experiment, even one he doubts, produces real data to change direction, whereas a sabotaged good idea teaches nothing.
points: Before resigning over strategy or priorities, ask whether the problem is specific to this company or a problem with companies in general.
Wójciszko's disagreement rule is to state the position and its consequences once or twice to the decision makers and then commit fully.
Continuing to argue after a decision is made brands a person a detractor, a reputation that outlasts the disagreement itself.
Divided loyalty produces three half-done strategies instead of one finished one, so nothing is learned.
Executing a weak option properly generates real feedback, which makes later course corrections evidence-based rather than opinion-based.
quotes: The uncomfortable part is that those problems rarely stay in the old office. They come with you. Different logo on the door, same frustrations by month six.
Every company has a manager someone thinks is clueless. Every company has a strategy someone thinks is wrong. Every company has priorities that move.
Everyone looks at the layer above or below and sees incompetence. That’s not a feature of your company. That’s a feature of how organizations are built.
My rule is simple. I’m obligated to say I disagree, out loud, in front of the people who make the decision. I explain what I’d do differently and what consequences I see.
You end up with three half-done strategies instead of one finished one. And you learn nothing from any of them.
A failed experiment that was executed well teaches you something. A good idea that was sabotaged halfway teaches you nothing.
Say what you think. Say it clearly, to the right people. Then let it go and do the work.
